**3B.9 Research Note**

Bottom line: Hasina’s 2024 crisis response was overwhelmingly coercive. The public record shows curfews, internet shutdowns, army deployment, blame-shifting, and lethal force risk. I found only weak counterevidence: internet service was restored after protests were called off, and the army reportedly refused to fire on civilians. Neither shows a genuinely protective domestic-crisis strategy.

- [Bangladesh blocks roads and internet, deploys army to curb protests](https://theprint.in/world/bangladesh-blocks-roads-and-internet-deploys-army-to-curb-protests/2183179/) — Reuters, July 20, 2024. Claim: Soldiers patrolled Dhaka, roadblocks went up, and internet/text services were suspended during the crackdown; this is coercive spectacle and censorship, not protection or restraint. IDs: `3B.9`, `3B.5`, `3B.6`, `3B.8`, `3B.1`, `2B.4`
- [Bangladesh PM Hasina blames opposition for violence, curfew to remain](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/bangladesh-pm-hasina-blames-opposition-for-violence-curfew-to-remain-3528153) — Reuters, July 22, 2024. Claim: Hasina kept the curfew in place and blamed political opponents for the violence, which reads as selective punishment and political fear management rather than crisis protection. IDs: `3B.9`, `3B.3`, `3B.5`, `3B.6`, `3B.8`, `2B.6`
- [Bangladesh’s crackdown on protesters left more than 170 dead, U.N. says](https://bangladesh.un.org/en/275065-bangladesh-t%C3%BCrk-decries-government-crackdown-urges-respect-international-human-rights) — United Nations / OHCHR, July 26, 2024. Claim: The UN said more than 170 people had been killed and warned that internet shutdowns increase impunity; that strongly supports the conclusion that the state response was abusive rather than protective. IDs: `3B.9`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.5`, `3B.6`, `2B.4`, `2B.9`
- [Bangladesh security forces target unarmed students](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/07/22/bangladesh-security-forces-target-unarmed-students) — Human Rights Watch, July 22, 2024. Claim: HRW reported security forces targeting unarmed students alongside Awami League-affiliated activists; this is direct evidence against a restraint-based response to a spontaneous flare-up. IDs: `3B.9`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.8`, `2B.4`, `2B.5`
- [Bangladesh prime minister Hasina resigns amid mass protests](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/08/06/bangladesh-prime-minister-hasina-resigns-amid-mass-protests) — Human Rights Watch, August 6, 2024. Claim: HRW described extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, and attacks on protesters during the crackdown; this is strong evidence that the crisis response amplified violence rather than suppressing it. IDs: `3B.9`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.8`, `2B.4`, `2B.9`
- [Bangladesh restores internet as students call off job-quota protests](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/bangladesh-restores-internet-as-students-call-off-jobquota-protests-3540555) — Reuters, July 29, 2024. Claim: Internet service was restored only after protesters called off the movement and conditions were said to be normalizing; this is the closest counterevidence, but it looks reactive and coercion-driven rather than a proactive protection strategy. IDs: `3B.9`, `3B.8`, `3B.5`, `3B.6`
- [Exclusive: Bangladesh army refused to suppress protest, sealing Hasina's fate](https://www.voanews.com/a/exclusive-bangladesh-army-refused-to-suppress-protest-sealing-hasina-s-fate/7733166.html) — Reuters, August 7, 2024. Claim: The army refused to open fire on civilians to enforce Hasina’s curfew; this is weak counterevidence showing a coercive option was resisted by the military, but it does not show Hasina herself chose restraint. IDs: `3B.9`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `3B.5`, `2B.9`
- [Bangladesh repression, security force abuses discredit elections](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/01/11/bangladesh-repression-security-force-abuses-discredit-elections) — Human Rights Watch, January 11, 2024. Claim: HRW reported arrests for criticism and widespread repression before the election, showing the year began with a punitive climate already in place. IDs: `3B.9`, `3B.8`, `3B.1`, `3B.2`, `2B.4`, `2B.5`

**Search Gap**
- I did not find credible evidence that Hasina used domestic-crisis powers to primarily protect civilians or suppress violence while preserving peaceful dissent.
- I also did not find evidence of a non-coercive, law-bound crisis doctrine comparable to restorative policing or rights-protective emergency management.
- The strongest available “on the other side” material is limited to de-escalation after protests collapsed, not an initial protective response.
